US disables ship trying to leave Iran, as Tehran vows to confront blockade

The US said the ship’s crew was unharmed, while Iran insisted its ports remained active and vowed to resist the blockade.

A projectile is headed to impact a vessel, after its crew attempted to run the US blockade of Iran, US Central Command said in a statement, in a location given as the Gulf of Oman, Nov 27, 2026. (Photo: REUTERS/US CENTRAL COMMAND)

DUBAI: The US military said on Friday (Nov 27) it disabled a commercial ship that attempted to run the US blockade of Iran, while an adviser to Iran' supreme leader said T ehran would keep the Strait of Hormuz shut and vowed to break the US embargo . US Central Command said in a statement that military aircraft launched precision munitions that struck the stern of the Palau-flagged M/V Pacific Archer in the Gulf of Oman on Thursday after it departed from the Iranian port city of Bandar Abbas. The ship’s propulsion was disabled while the civilian crew was unharmed, Central Command said. The US reimposed its naval blockade on Iranian ports in July, and earlier this month announced Task Force Iron Gate to restrict the movement of weapons and sanctioned materials across Iran's land borders and the Caspian Sea. Mohammad Mokhber, an adviser to Iran's Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei, vowed on Friday to break the embargo, according to Iranian state media. "Neither will the Strait of Hormuz be reopened, nor will we allow the blockade to remain in place," state media reported Mokhber saying. He did not give details of Iran's plans for breaking the embargo. Separately, Iranian navy commander Shahram Irani told state television: "Breaking through the enemy blockade is underway and our ports are active today. Contrary to all propaganda, maritime escorts are taking place and we stand with the shipowners and sailors." "The enemy's attempt is to cut off the lifeblood of our economy in whatever way it can, and this has so far failed," Irani said, without giving details.

NAIROBI: A Kenyan court found starvation cult leader Paul Mackenzie guilty of manslaughter on Friday (Nov 27) for the deaths of 123 of his followers, the latest conviction over one of the deadliest cult-related massacres in modern times. Mackenzie , already serving a 200-year jail sentence from earlier this month for the murder of nearly 200 children, has also been convicted of child cruelty, assault, radicalisation and terrorism-related offences. The preacher led an apocalyptic Christian church in a forest near Kenya's Indian Ocean coast, telling his followers to starve themselves and their children to death to reach heaven before the end of the world. His suspected 500 victims included children buried alive or dumped in latrines.

Delivering his judgement in a court in the city of Mombasa, magistrate Alex Ithuku said Mackenzie "gave the directions to fast to death ... the order in which people were to die, directed the faithful move to secluded fasting places, and took part in what followed these deaths". Mackenzie had pleaded not guilty to manslaughter, and one of his lawyers said he would appeal it after sentencing. The scale of the killings in the Shakahola Forest, which gradually emerged from April 2023 onwards, has shocked Kenya and prompted calls for tighter oversight of religious groups. In 2023, President William Ruto said he took responsibility as head of state for the government's failure to prevent the deaths. Comparable mass killings include a doomsday cult that killed more than 700 people in Uganda in 2000 and a 1978 massacre in Guyana, where an American cult leader killed over 900 people by ordering them to drink poison.

OSLO: Airline Norse Atlantic’s Norwegian operating unit has declared bankruptcy, the long-haul budget carrier said on Friday (Nov 27), succumbing to soaring fuel costs wrought by the war in Iran. Norse Atlantic ASA, which is listed on the Oslo Euronext Expand bourse, and other group companies are not part of the filing and are still attempting to stay in business, the company said in a statement. Norse Atlantic, which launched in 2022, on Nov 25 warned that its financial situation was “critical”. The following day, it said it had suspended all flights and that the board could file for bankruptcy unless it urgently secured funding.

“The Board of Norse Atlantic Airways AS has made the difficult decision to file for bankruptcy despite extensive efforts from the company and the group to find a solution,” Norse CEO Eivind Roald said in a statement. “The board, management and advisers of the listed entity Norse Atlantic ASA and the UK subsidiary are working to find a solution for the remaining part of the business to continue operations,” Roald said. Earlier on Nov 27, Norse said its lessors had terminated their leasing contracts for all 12 aircraft in the carrier’s fleet, demanding that the planes be handed back, a claim contested by the company. Norse in 2021 signed long-term leases for nine Boeing 787 Dreamliner aircraft from Ireland-based AerCap Holdings and six Dreamliners from Singapore-based BOC Aviation. It later returned three of the planes to AerCap. “The company contests the validity of the termination notices,” Norse said in a statement. The AerCap leases were due to run for about 12 years for each aircraft, while the BOC contracts were due to run for 16 years, according to Norse’s latest annual report. “Although they are contesting the notices, it sounds pretty decisive. Unless successful in this, they will not be able to resume operations,” said aviation analyst John Strickland. The global aviation industry is suffering its worst crisis since the Covid-19 pandemic as the US-Iran conflict, which began at the end of February, disrupts operations, drives up fuel prices, and sends airlines’ costs skyrocketing .

AMSTERDAM: Dutch authorities seized 26 critically endangered Vallarta mud turtles at Schiphol airport last week, the Dutch Food and Consumer Product Safety Authority (NVWA) said on Friday (Nov 27). The Vallarta turtles, one of the world's smallest turtle species, were brought in from Mexico, where only around 300 of them remain in the wild. They were hidden in the checked baggage of a man who was travelling to Hong Kong, the NVWA said. The man was arrested and further investigations are ongoing. Wrapped in duct tape to prevent them from moving, most of the turtles were packed in a box together with a toy car, while a few others were placed inside a sealed sock. NVWA said they all survived and were taken to a specialist animal rescue centre. Vallarta mud turtles can sell for up to US$30,000 each, the US-based Center for Biological Diversity said last month in a statement calling on the Mexican government to do more to protect the animals.

LONDON: The British government department which ad minister s pensions and welfare payments said on Friday (Nov 27) t hat a "serious" cyber incident had prompted it to take services offline but that so far no personal data had been found to be compromised . "This is a serious cyber incident. The investigation into the causes is ongoing," work and pensions minister McFadden told UK media when asked if a malicious attack could be the cause. Regular benefit and pension payments were continuing as normal, he said, adding that the department was working with the National Cyber Security Centre and other government officials to get services back up and running as soon as possible. "The most important message for the public at the moment is that there is no evidence that anyone's personal details have been compromised," he said. A spokesperson for British Prime Minister Andy Burnham had earlier said there was no other evidence that a malicious actor had targeted any other government departments. British companies and institutions have been increasingly hit by aggressive and regular cyber attacks in recent years, with some suffering months of disruption, including the British Library, a blood testing service, the London Underground, Marks & Spencer, the Co-op and Jaguar Land Rover.

FAST

SYDNEY: An Australian woman convicted of murdering three of her estranged husband's relatives with a meal laced with deadly mushrooms on Friday (Nov 27) filed an appeal bid with Australia's top court. Erin Patterson was convicted last year of killing her three elderly in-laws by feeding them beef Wellington laced with death cap mushrooms, in a case that gripped Australia. Last month, the Court of Appeal in the Supreme Court of Victoria rejected Patterson's attempt to quash her conviction. The High Court is her last opportunity to appeal her conviction. Patterson has consistently maintained her innocence, saying the deaths were an accident. Patterson's application to the High Court rests on some of the same grounds as her Supreme Court action, according to court documents.

A general view of Erin Patterson’s house in Leongatha, Australia, on Jun 24, 2025. (Photo: Reuters/Asanka Brendon Ratnayake)

"The Court of Appeal erred in its application of principles that justice must not only be done, but be seen to be done," said Patterson's appeal bid, filed by her lawyers on Friday.   The grounds include arguments that some evidence should have been excluded from the trial and that the jury's accidental accommodation in the same hotel as other people involved in the case undermined the verdict. Patterson initially received a life sentence with a minimum of 33 years before being eligible for parole, but the prosecution appealed, arguing that it was inadequate in light of the seriousness of the crimes. Victoria's Supreme Court last month upheld the prosecution's appeal and sentenced Patterson to life without parole — only the second time in Australian history such a sentence has been handed down to a woman.  A jury last year found Patterson invited her mother-in-law Gail Patterson, father-in-law Donald Patterson and Gail’s sister, Heather Wilkinson, to a 2023 lunch at her home in Leongatha, a town of about 6,000 people, some 135km southeast of Melbourne, and fed them the poisoned lunch. She was also convicted of the attempted murder of Ian Wilkinson, Heather’s husband, who survived the meal. The 11-week trial, held in the nearby country town of Morwell, attracted worldwide attention, and the case has since spawned several podcasts and books.

Source: Reuters/lk

SEOUL: Iran's foreign minister has told his South Korean counterpart that a foreign military presence in the Gulf region would heighten tensions rather than contribute to peace, as Seoul prepares to expand the operational area of a navy unit to waters south of the Gulf of Oman. Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi spoke by telephone on Thursday (Nov 26) with South Korea's Cho Hyun, who reaffirmed Seoul did not intend to join any war or deploy troops to the Gulf, the Iranian embassy in Seoul said in an X post on Friday. South Korea's parliament is reviewing a government motion to broaden the operating area of its Cheonghae naval unit to include the outer waters of the Gulf of Oman to help ensure safe navigation of its commercial vessels. The anti-piracy Cheonghae unit has been stationed in the Gulf of Aden since 2009. Araqchi said the presence of foreign militaries "would instead heighten tensions and expand the scope of conflict", the Iranian embassy said. South Korea's Foreign Ministry said Cho explained that the mission of the navy unit was to ensure the safety of South Koreans and protect the country's economic interests. South Korea, which is one of the world's largest oil and gas importers, sourced 70 per cent of its oil from the Middle East in 2025, with most shipments delivered through the Strait of Hormuz , according to government data.

WELLINGTON: New Zealand’s ruling centre-right coalition has narrowly missed winning a parliamentary majority, final election results showed on Friday (Nov 27), leaving Prime Minister Christopher Luxon needing the support of the centrist Opportunity Party to remain in power. If Luxon cannot reach either a coalition or confidence-and-supply deal, and any negotiations between other parties fail to produce a majority government, New Zealand will have to hold fresh elections. Electoral Commission results showed the coalition with 65 seats, one seat short of a majority in the 130-seat parliament. "New Zealanders need a government that is stable, that works together and will last for the full term," Luxon told a news conference.

"Kiwis won’t thank us for rushing to an agreement that falls apart or for sending them back to the polls." OPPORTUNITY TO NEGOTIATE WITH NATIONAL Luxon’s centre-right National Party secured 40 seats in the Nov 7 election, and its junior coalition partners ACT and New Zealand First won 13 seats and 12 seats, respectively. Labour, the largest opposition party, won 36 seats. New entrant to parliament Opportunity won seven seats, and its leader Qiulae Wong said on Friday she would negotiate with National as the party with the largest number of seats. "I don't think anybody can rule anything out at this stage because we haven't had any discussions," Wong told a press conference, adding all options were on the table including being on the crossbenches.

"We are going to do everything we can to make sure that there is a stable government," she said. Opportunity's platform includes stronger climate commitments, a ban on bottom-trawling fishing, tighter competition rules and a more interventionist approach to public investment, policies that cut against parts of the coalition's agenda. ACT Party leader David Seymour said government formation could happen "quite rapidly" if the parties involved worked together to come to an agreement. "The government can be formed if the coalition is prepared to work with Opportunity at some level," he said in an interview with 1News. The results show a centre-left coalition of Labour, the Green Party and Te Pati Maori would not be able to form a government, even with the support of Opportunity. However, if NZ First were to strike a deal with the centre-left parties — as it did with Labour after the 2017 election — they could form a coalition government. The New Zealand dollar, which hit a 17-year low against the US dollar this week, strengthened slightly after the announcement of the election results. Earlier this month, preliminary results from the Electoral Commission had shown the ruling coalition with a majority of two seats. The final tally includes special votes, which include those from people voting overseas or outside their electorate, and typically skew left. The Electoral Commission said there were 2,931,604 votes cast, of which 484,865 were special votes.

Thanksgiving storm knocks out power, disrupts flights on US East Coast

Strong winds of up to 70 mph caused over 400 flight cancellations and power outages affecting hundreds of thousands across the US East Coast.

NEW YORK: A powerful storm disrupted the Thanksgiving holiday along much of the US East Coast on Thursday (Nov 26), knocking out power for hundreds of thousands of users as wind gusts of up to 70 mph (112 kph) toppled trees and power lines. Heavy rains flooded coastal areas, while utilities warned that rain-soaked ground and strong winds could increase the risk of falling trees and power outages. Nearly 200,000 homes and businesses had no power in Virginia and another 177,000 in Maryland as of 2:26pm ET (Friday, 3.26am, Singapore time) according to poweroutage.us, which also showed Pennsylvania, New Jersey and North Carolina each had tens of thousands of utility customers without electricity . Utilities and state officials had warned the combination of strong onshore winds and rain could cause widespread power disruptions.

Wind gusts of 50 to 70 mph were reported or forecast across parts of Virginia, Maryland, Delaware, New Jersey, New York, and coastal New England, according to the US National Weather Service. New York City Emergency Management reported winds intensified on Thursday afternoon, reaching 56 mph (90 kph) at LaGuardia Airport. The NWS said strong onshore winds associated with the storm, combined with king tides, were causing coastal flooding in low-lying communities along portions of the East Coast.

A person holds onto their upturned umbrella while crossing the street during high winds and rain during a Thanksgiving Day storm in New York City, US, November 26, 2026. REUTERS/Adam Gray

The threat of storms had already led officials to postpone Thursday's 100th edition of the annual Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade in New York City, marking the first time the event has been rescheduled due to severe weather. The storm also disrupted holiday air travel, with more than 400 US flights canceled and some 1,600 delayed by early on Thursday afternoon, according to FlightAware. Major airports in the Washington and New York City areas were among the hardest hit. "A powerful coastal storm will continue to bring severe impacts to the region through today into this evening due to damaging high winds accompanied by heavy rainfall," the NWS said. "The storm departs overnight into Friday."

Source: Reuters/fs

Crew member dies after diesel tanker capsizes off Ibiza, no pollution so far

The tanker carried up to 7,000 tonnes of diesel, but authorities reported no major spill and activated Spain’s Level 2 maritime pollution response plan.

MADRID: At least one crew member aboard a ship carrying diesel has died after the vessel capsized and partially sank off the Spanish island of Ibiza on Thursday (Nov 26), regional authorities said , adding there were no signs of pollution so far. The Malta-flagged chemical tanker Med Emre was sailing from Algeciras to Barcelona and may have been carrying up to 7,000 metric tons of diesel when it keeled over about 30 nautical miles (56 km) off Ibiza 's northwestern coast, the Balearic Islands' interior department said. Emergency services said all 17 crew members were rescued, but one died after being taken directly to Ibiza 's Can Misses hospital. Six others were brought to Ibiza airport and taken to two hospitals with light injuries, primarily hypothermia. Of the remaining crew, five were taken to Valencia and five remained in good condition aboard a rescue vessel, they added.

Pablo Garriz, the Balearic Islands' regional head of emergencies, said the crew included Turkish and Indian nationals, but he could not yet confirm the nationality of the deceased. The tanker remained partially submerged with its keel protruding above the surface, Garriz told reporters, despite initial indications that it had sunk completely. "The positive news is that the vessel is not on the seabed but remains semi-submerged at the surface, which allows salvage and containment operations," he said, adding there was currently no impact on Balearic waters or coastline and no evidence of a significant spill, although small sheens had been observed. Technical experts were assessing the vessel's stability before deciding on salvage and cargo-recovery operations, he added.

Spain's maritime rescue service sent an aircraft and a vessel specialised in oil-spill response, the Clara Campoamor, to survey the area. Three helicopters took part in the rescue, along with nearby merchant vessels. Spain's merchant marine authority activated the national maritime pollution contingency plan at level 2, the second-highest. The waters surrounding Ibiza are a habitat for sea turtles, dolphins and the Balearic shearwater, one of Europe's most threatened seabirds. The area is also home to extensive meadows of Posidonia oceanica seagrass, which plays a vital role in supporting marine biodiversity. Spain's worst maritime environmental disaster occurred in 2002, when the Bahamas-flagged tanker Prestige sank off the northwestern Galicia region, spilling tens of thousands of tons of heavy fuel oil and fouling hundreds of beaches in Spain and France. The Balearic regional government said it was gathering information on the accident and its possible consequences, including any risk of fuel pollution, before deciding on further measures.

Source: Reuters/fs

RIYADH: The Saudi - led military coalition fighting Yemen's Houthis said on Thursday (Nov 26) that the Iran-aligned group had attacked Saudi Aramco's Jazan refinery, a day after hitting the largest oil refinery in the kingdom. The refinery in the southwestern city of Jazan, near the Yemeni border, is designed to process up to 400,000 barrels of crude oil per day. The coalition said it had later destroyed a ballistic missile launch platform in the Yemeni port city of Hodeidah, which it said the Houthis had used in Thursday's attack on the refinery. Earlier it said that targeting civilians and civilian infrastructure would be met with a firm military response.

On Wednesday the Houthis claimed attacks on Ras Tanura, Saudi Arabia's largest refinery and a major crude export hub, and the Red Sea ports of Jeddah and Jazan. The Saudi - led coalition said it had intercepted four drones over Ras Tanura and air defences had destroyed a drone near Jeddah Islamic Port. The Houthis , who control the most populous areas of Yemen including the capital Sanaa, have launched missiles and drones at Saudi airports, oil facilities and office buildings since Yemen's civil war reignited in July, in a spillover from the US-Iran war. The attacks have previously temporarily disrupted some of Aramco's operations and caused the cancellation of most international flights to Riyadh. They also forced Saudi Arabia to postpone or cancel major international events, including soccer's AFC Asian Cup and the flagship FII investment conference. Fighting has intensified since the Houthis seized strategic territory along Yemen's Red Sea coast in September and advanced towards the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a vital shipping route for Gulf oil producers seeking access to the Red Sea.
